passage:
Saturday
Dear Diary,
We WON again! 3-1 against Green House. I wore my red shirt, the one with the torn pocket. That makes four wins in the red shirt. The two times we lost, it was in the wash. So it is the shirt. It must be.
Urmila akka says that's silly. She says we won today because Irfan came back from his holiday and he's our best goalie. And Green House had only nine players. I told her she doesn't understand football.
Amma says I can't wear it every day because it smells. I'm going to wash it myself on Friday night so it's ready for the final.
- Darshan (Amma's lucky boy)

qa.q: What was today's score, and against which team?
qa.a: 3-1 against Green House.

qa.q: Why is Darshan so sure the red shirt makes the team win?
qa.a: He has seen four wins with the shirt on and losses when it was in the wash, so the pattern feels like proof, and he enjoys feeling lucky.

qa.q: What could help Darshan test his idea?
qa.a: He could write down each match with who played, how many players the other team had and what he wore, and see whether things like Irfan being back matter more.

qa.q: How does Urmila akka see the red shirt?
qa.a: She thinks it's silly and sees other reasons for the win: Irfan being back in goal and Green House having only nine players.

grounding: It shows a boy linking his red shirt to his team's wins just because the two keep happening together.

passage:
In Vadipatti, the under-12 kabaddi team practised on the dry field behind the temple. Muthu had noticed something. Every match he played in his faded red shirt, the team won. The week it tore and he wore blue, they lost to the next village.
"It's the shirt," he told his sister Shalini, holding it up like a flag. "It brings the luck."
Shalini, sewing the tear by lamplight, looked up. "That week, wasn't Selvam down with fever? And Kavitha teacher had gone to her mother's village, so nobody made you practise."
Muthu frowned. "That's also true."
"So which one did it, the shirt or the missing people?"
He pulled the shirt on anyway. "Maybe both. I'm not taking the chance."

qa.q: What happened the week Muthu wore blue?
qa.a: They lost to the next village.

qa.q: Why does Muthu still pull the shirt on after Shalini's questions?
qa.a: He half sees her point, but the pattern of wins still feels real, and wearing the shirt feels safer than risking a loss.

qa.q: How could Kavitha teacher help the team think about the shirt?
qa.a: She could list with them what was different on the losing day, like Selvam being ill and no practice, so they see other reasons for winning and losing.

qa.q: What would change if Muthu kept wearing the red shirt but the team stopped practising?
qa.a: They might start losing even with the shirt on, which would show that the shirt was never what made them win.

grounding: It shows a village boy deciding his red shirt causes wins because the shirt and the wins appeared together.

passage:
Tariq pulled the red T-shirt over his head and tucked it under his team vest. It was Thursday in the sports hall in Leeds, and the Hawks had won every game he'd worn it.
"You're wearing that again?" Liam asked, lacing his trainers.
"Five games, five wins. It's the shirt."
"We also got Coach Dunn five games ago," Liam said. "She's the one who makes us do passing drills every Tuesday."
Tariq tugged at the collar. That was true too. But the red shirt felt warm and lucky, like it was on his side.
They won again, 22-18. Liam scored eight of the points.
In the changing room, Tariq folded the shirt carefully. "See?"
Liam just shook his head and grinned.

qa.q: What was the score of Thursday's game?
qa.a: They won again, 22-18.

qa.q: What does Tariq's careful folding of the shirt suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he treats the shirt as special and truly believes it helps, because the lucky feeling is comforting even after Liam's point about the coach.

qa.q: What might Liam say to help Tariq see what is really changing the results?
qa.a: Liam could point out that the wins began when Coach Dunn started the Tuesday passing drills, and suggest trying one game without the shirt.

qa.q: How might Coach Dunn feel if the team gave the red shirt the credit?
qa.a: She might feel a little overlooked, since her passing drills may be doing much of the work.

grounding: It shows a boy crediting his red T-shirt for his team's winning run because the two happened together.

passage:
At the Saturday relay practice at the community sports club, Coach Nair called out the teams. Zubin, ten, came out of the changing room in his red T-shirt, the one with the faded number 7.
"You wore that last week too," Afreen said, tying her laces.
"Because we won last week. And the week before. Both times, red shirt." Zubin counted on his fingers. "The time we lost, it was in the wash. So it's the shirt."
"We also had Kartik back last week. He's the fastest."
"That's different. Kartik is just one person. The shirt is every time."
When his team won again, Zubin tugged the shirt proudly and told the coach he would wear it to the district meet. Afreen rolled her eyes and went to drink water.

qa.q: What number was on Zubin's red T-shirt?
qa.a: A faded number 7.

qa.q: How does Zubin feel about his red shirt, and what shows it?
qa.a: Zubin feels confident and proud about the shirt, tugging it after the win and planning to wear it to the district meet, because every win he remembers came with it.

qa.q: What could help Zubin check whether the shirt really matters?
qa.a: He could keep a simple list of races with and without the shirt, and also note who ran each time, to see what really changed the result.

qa.q: How does Afreen see Zubin's red-shirt idea?
qa.a: Afreen thinks Kartik coming back explains the wins better and finds the shirt idea silly, which shows in the eye-roll.

grounding: It shows a boy noticing his team wins when he wears his red shirt and deciding the shirt causes the wins.

passage:
I'm Kalyani, and I stayed with my aunt's family in Jaipur for the summer. My cousin Hrishi, nine, has a red shirt he calls "the match shirt". On every night his football club played on TV, he put it on before dinner.
The first week the club won twice, and he said, "See? Red shirt, win." On Thursday Ritu, his little sister, hid the shirt as a joke. The club lost. Hrishi was furious with her, really furious, and said she had made them lose.
I don't know if he truly believed it or just needed someone to blame. But by Sunday he was checking the shirt was clean on Saturday night.
Ritu whispered to me that the club's best player had been injured on Thursday. She said it very quietly, like she didn't want Hrishi to hear.

qa.q: What did Ritu do on Thursday?
qa.a: She hid the shirt as a joke.

qa.q: Why might Hrishi be so sure the shirt made the club lose?
qa.a: The shirt and the wins kept showing up together, so when the shirt was missing and the club lost, it felt like proof to Hrishi that one caused the other.

qa.q: How could Kalyani help Hrishi see what else happened on Thursday?
qa.a: Kalyani could calmly bring up the injured best player and ask Hrishi which seems more likely to change a match, a shirt at home or a missing player.

qa.q: What is it like for Ritu to be blamed for the loss?
qa.a: Ritu probably feels hurt and a bit scared of Hrishi's anger, which is why she whispers about the injured player instead of saying it out loud 😔

grounding: It shows a boy linking his red shirt to his team's wins and deciding the shirt causes them, because the two happen together.

passage:
Coach's note, under-11 football, Saturday.
Kamal turned up again in his faded red shirt, the one with the torn sleeve. When I asked him to wear the team bib over it, he refused, close to tears. "We win when I wear it. We won three times!" His teammate Seema told me he hasn't washed it in two weeks so the luck doesn't come out. I sat with him on the bench and we looked at the fixture list together: those three wins were against the two weakest teams in the league, and we lost last month when he wore it too; he'd forgotten. Kamal went quiet, then asked, "So maybe it's because we practised?" I said practice and the easier games probably did more. He put the bib on. I'll keep an eye on how he takes the next loss.

qa.q: What did Seema tell the coach about the red shirt?
qa.a: Seema said Kamal hasn't washed it in two weeks so the luck doesn't come out.

qa.q: Why did the red shirt feel so important to Kamal?
qa.a: Kamal felt anxious about losing his luck, because the wins and the shirt kept showing up together, so it felt like the shirt made them happen.

qa.q: What helped Kamal loosen his belief, and what could the coach try next?
qa.a: Looking at the fixture list showed the wins came against weak teams and that he had also lost in the shirt; next the coach could chart practice and results with him.

qa.q: What might it be like for Seema to watch Kamal and the shirt?
qa.a: Seema may find it a bit funny and a bit worrying, which may be why the unwashed shirt got mentioned to the coach.

grounding: Shows a child deciding a shirt causes wins because the two happened together, and a coach checking the fixtures with him.

passage: Dear Diary, Tanvir here, and I have made a BIG discovery. Every time Nani comes from Lucknow, it rains. Last July she came: rain. In September: rain. Today she got off the train and the clouds opened right over the station! So Nani makes it rain. I told my friend Lakshmi from next door, and we planned to ask Nani to visit in May, when the tank at school is dry. Lakshmi said maybe Nani just comes in the rainy months because that's when the holidays are. I said no, it is Nani. Then Abbu reminded me that Nani came in December too, and it didn't rain once. Hmm. I am still keeping a chart at the back of this diary. Nani laughed and said she only brings pickles. 🙂

qa.q: Where did it rain when Nani arrived today?
qa.a: The clouds opened right over the station.

qa.q: Why does Tanvir feel sure that Nani makes it rain?
qa.a: Tanvir feels excited and proud of the discovery, because the visits Tanvir remembers came with rain, so the two things seem joined.

qa.q: What could Tanvir's chart help check?
qa.a: The chart could list every visit, rainy or dry, including December, so Tanvir can see whether rain follows Nani or just the rainy months.

qa.q: How does Lakshmi explain the rain differently?
qa.a: Lakshmi thinks Nani probably visits in the rainy months because the holidays fall then, so the season brings both.

grounding: Shows a child deciding a grandmother's visits cause rain because the two kept happening together.

passage: In Rasulpur, the kite fights happened every evening on the flat roof of the grain store. Farhan, ten, had decided it was the tamarind tree. "When I sit under it before flying, I win," he told his sister Ayesha, tugging her to the spot. "Four times. Four!" Ayesha squinted at the sky. "You only sit there on windy evenings, when everyone's out flying. And your kite does better in strong wind." Farhan frowned. "No. The tree helps." That evening there was no wind at all. He sat under the tamarind for a long time anyway; then his kite drooped and was cut within a minute. Walking home, he kicked a stone and muttered, "Maybe it's the wind." Ayesha grinned but didn't say I told you so.

qa.q: Where did the kite fights happen every evening?
qa.a: They happened on the flat roof of the grain store.

qa.q: Why did the tamarind tree feel lucky to Farhan?
qa.a: Farhan felt hopeful and sure because the tree and his wins came together four times, so it seemed the tree was helping.

qa.q: What could Farhan test to find out what really helps his kite?
qa.a: He could skip the tree on a windy evening and sit under it on a calm one, and see whether the wins follow the tree or the wind.

qa.q: What would change if Ayesha had said 'I told you so'?
qa.a: Farhan might have felt embarrassed and defended the tree harder, instead of reaching the idea about the wind by himself.

grounding: Shows a child crediting a tree for kite wins when both really came with windy evenings.

passage: Hiroshi had a red T-shirt with a small tiger on it. In Osaka, his football team had won the last three Saturdays, and each time, Hiroshi had worn the tiger shirt. "It's the shirt," he told Daniel, the goalkeeper. "When I wear it, we win." Daniel shrugged. "Maybe." On the fourth Saturday, the shirt was in the wash. Hiroshi was sure they would lose. He played nervously, looking at his plain blue shirt. They won anyway, 2–0. He didn't understand. The next Saturday he wore the tiger shirt, and they lost 1–3. Coach sat everyone down. "We won three because the other teams were weak. We lost today because this team is strong." Hiroshi looked at his tiger. "So it's not the shirt?" "It's the other team," Coach said.

qa.q: What was on Hiroshi's red T-shirt?
qa.a: A small tiger.

qa.q: Why was Hiroshi nervous on the fourth Saturday?
qa.a: He felt anxious because his tiger shirt was in the wash, and he believed the shirt caused the team's wins.

qa.q: What did Coach help Hiroshi see, and what could he look at next time?
qa.a: That wins and losses came from how strong the other teams were; next time he can look for other reasons behind a pattern.

qa.q: How does Daniel seem to see the shirt?
qa.a: Daniel seems unconvinced, just shrugging and saying "Maybe".

grounding: Shows a child deciding his red shirt causes his team's wins because the two happened together, until results and his coach show otherwise.

passage: In the school sports office, Kunal told Rashmi ma'am his secret. "On days I wear my red socks, our kho-kho team wins. Every time." She checked the chart on the wall. Their team had won four matches. "Which days did you wear the red socks?" "All four!" "And which teams did we play on those days?" Kunal looked at the chart. The names were the smaller schools. "And the day we lost?" "I... wore blue socks. Against St. Mary's." "Who are the district champions?" "St. Mary's." Rashmi ma'am smiled. "So the socks and the wins came together. But what else came with the wins?" Kunal thought. "Easy teams?" "So what really made us win?" He grinned slowly. "Maybe not the socks."

qa.q: Which team did they lose to?
qa.a: St. Mary's.

qa.q: What was Kunal feeling when he told Rashmi ma'am his secret?
qa.a: He felt excited and proud, sure his red socks made the team win because they always came together.

qa.q: How did Rashmi ma'am help Kunal find the real reason?
qa.a: She asked which teams they played on red-sock days, so he saw that easy opponents came with the wins too.

qa.q: How might Rashmi ma'am see Kunal's belief?
qa.a: She seems amused and kind, using it to teach him to look for other reasons behind a pattern.

grounding: Shows a child believing his red socks cause his team's wins because they happen together, until a teacher points out the easier opponents.

passage:
Monday. Chetan's cricket team won, and he'd worn his red cap. Tuesday, another win. "It's the cap," he told Kunal. "Red cap, we win."
Thursday. Chetan forgot the red cap. They lost. "See!" he said. "Told you."
Saturday. Kunal's father, who coached the team, heard about the cap. He wrote down every match of the month: red cap or not, win or lose, and who bowled. Chetan looked at it. Three wins with the cap. One loss without. But also: in every win, Kunal's big brother had bowled. In the loss, he had been away at his exam. Chetan stared at the notebook. "So it was bhaiya, not my cap?" "Maybe," said the coach. "Want to test it? Wear the cap next week when he's away."

qa.q: How many wins did Chetan have with the red cap?
qa.a: Three wins with the cap.

qa.q: What was Chetan feeling when he said "See! Told you"?
qa.a: He felt certain and a little triumphant, believing the lost match proved the cap caused the wins.

qa.q: What did the coach's notebook show, and how could Chetan test it?
qa.a: That Kunal's big brother bowled in every win and was away for the loss; Chetan could wear the cap when the brother is away to test it.

qa.q: How might Kunal feel when the notebook points to his brother?
qa.a: Kunal might feel proud of his brother and a little amused at Chetan's cap theory.

grounding: Shows over a week a child believing his red cap causes wins because they come together, until a notebook shows another cause.

passage:
Kamal, you won't take off that blue cap because your team wins when you wear it? Sit. I'm your Sunaina Thamma, and I've seen this before, with your Papa.
When he was ten, every Durga Puja the boys of our para played football behind the pandal. One year your Papa got a new red shirt as a Puja gift, and his team won. He wore it the next evening. They won again. After that he wouldn't let me wash it. By Navami it smelled like a goat.
On Dashami it rained, the field turned to mud, and his team lost. He cried, "Ma, you touched the shirt and spoiled it."
I asked him, "On the days you won, was the ground dry? Your team is small and quick. What happens to small, quick boys in mud?"
He sat very still. Then he let me wash the shirt.

qa.q: What did Kamal's Papa get as a Puja gift?
qa.a: Kamal's Papa got a new red shirt as a Puja gift.

qa.q: Why did Kamal's Papa refuse to have the red shirt washed?
qa.a: He felt hopeful and sure, since the wins came on the days he wore it, so washing it felt like washing away the luck.

qa.q: Which question turned things around, and why?
qa.a: Asking whether the ground was dry on the winning days pointed to the weather and the team's quick players as a likelier cause than the shirt.

qa.q: How might Thamma have felt when accused of spoiling the shirt?
qa.a: Thamma was probably amused and tender, understanding the boy's disappointment while gently looking for the real reason.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling a boy who believed his red shirt made his team win because the two happened together.

passage:
In the thick December fog, the school bus in Shillong was late again, crawling up the hill with its lights on.
"Test today," Joseph groaned to Rajni as they waited, stamping their cold feet. "Every time the bus is late, Ma'am gives a surprise test. Three times already."
"Every time?"
"Monday, Monday and Monday. The bus was late all three. So the late bus makes her cross, and she gives tests."
Rajni wiped her glasses. "What day is it today?"
"Monday."
"And why is the bus late on Mondays?"
Joseph thought. "The driver takes the market road. Market day."
"And when does Ma'am give tests?"
"...On Mondays. She says weekends make us forget." He frowned at the fog. "So it's Monday doing both things."
The bus finally arrived, twenty minutes late. There was a test.

qa.q: Why is the bus late on Mondays?
qa.a: The driver takes the market road on Mondays because it is market day.

qa.q: Why did Joseph feel sure the late bus caused the tests?
qa.a: Joseph was grumpy and convinced, because three late buses matched three surprise tests, so the two things seemed linked.

qa.q: What question helped Joseph find the real link, and what could he ask next time?
qa.a: Asking what day it was showed Monday caused both; next time Joseph could ask whether some third thing makes two events happen together.

qa.q: How does Rajni see Joseph's theory?
qa.a: Rajni sees it as a mix-up and patiently asks questions so Joseph finds the answer himself.

grounding: Shows a child deciding that a late bus causes surprise tests because the two happen together, until he sees Monday explains both.

passage:
The week before Holi, Gurpreet's Nani fried gujiya in the colony's shared kitchen, and the smell reached the cricket game between the parked cars in Jaipur.
"Every time Nani makes gujiya, we win," Gautam said, licking sugar off his fingers. "Last Sunday, gujiya, win. The Sunday before, gujiya, win. Today, gujiya."
"So gujiya scores runs?" Gurpreet asked.
"They go together. That's proof."
Gurpreet thought about it. "When does Nani make them?"
"Sundays."
"And who plays on Sundays?"
Gautam counted. "Everyone. No tuition, no school. All eleven of us."
"And on weekdays?"
"Seven, if we're lucky." Gautam stopped chewing. "So Sunday brings the gujiya and the full team. The gujiya just turns up with the win."
"Still eating it, though," Gurpreet said, holding out the plate.

qa.q: On which day does Nani make gujiya?
qa.a: Nani makes gujiya on Sundays.

qa.q: Why did Gautam feel sure the gujiya caused the wins?
qa.a: Gautam felt confident and happy because gujiya and wins had come together two Sundays in a row, so they seemed linked.

qa.q: What question could Gautam ask the next time two things happen together?
qa.a: Gautam could ask what else is different on those days, like the full team on Sundays, before deciding one causes the other.

qa.q: How does Gurpreet see the gujiya idea?
qa.a: Gurpreet is amused but curious, and asks questions until Gautam spots that Sunday brings both the gujiya and the full team.

grounding: Shows a child deciding festival sweets cause his team's wins because they happen on the same days, until a third factor appears.

passage:
